spoken: At Carthage, by the sea, white crosses and Stars of David stand in straight lines.
At Medjez-el-Bab, west of Tunis, matching headstones stand row after row.
On the heights of Gammarth, north of Tunis, crosses and steles stand in rows.
And at Borj Sedria there are no rows at all, only six stone courtyards on a hillside.
And many who died in that war have no such place. This film visits the four, and looks beyond them.
From November 1942 to May 1943, the war crossed Tunisia, then a French protectorate under the Bey of Tunis.
German and Italian troops occupied Tunis, Bizerte and the east, and British, Commonwealth, American and French armies fought them.
Tunisians of every faith, Muslims, Jews and Christians, lived through the occupation, the bombing and the fighting.
After the war, each country chose how to gather its dead, and how to mark their graves.
Four of these cemeteries lie within about 60 kilometres of Tunis.
Our first stop is Carthage, where the North Africa American Cemetery covers part of the ancient Roman city.
It is run by the American Battle Monuments Commission, an agency of the United States government.
It was set up in 1948, on land Tunisia granted free and for ever, and dedicated in 1960.
On 27 acres, 2,833 headstones stand in straight lines, in nine plots, with pools where the paths cross.
Of these, 2,777 are Latin crosses and 56 are Stars of David.
Most of those honoured here died in operations from North Africa to the Persian Gulf, not only in Tunisia.
Along the mall, the Tablets of the Missing run for 364 feet, about 111 metres.
They name 3,724 men missing on land, at sea and in the air, more than the graves here.
A rosette beside a name marks a man who has since been found and identified.
About 60 kilometres west of Tunis, Medjez-el-Bab stayed on the front line from December 1942 until the Allied advances of spring 1943.
Today it has Tunisia's largest Commonwealth war cemetery, run by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.
The Commission counts 2,903 servicemen buried or commemorated here, and 385 of the burials are unidentified.
Its headstones are all alike, whatever a man's rank, race or faith, each with a badge, a name and a religious symbol.
At Medjez, a memorial names almost 2,000 more men of the First and Eighth Armies who have no known grave.
Across Tunisia, the Commission keeps eight war cemeteries, from Tabarka to Sfax.
North of Tunis, on the heights of Gammarth, France opened a military cemetery on 5 January 1944.
The French army in Tunisia included Tunisian, Algerian and Moroccan tirailleurs, as well as Europeans.
Its dead were buried by faith, and Gammarth took Christians, Jews and other non-Muslims.
Muslim soldiers, many of them tirailleurs, were buried in Muslim cemeteries, such as those at Haffouz and Tarf esh-Shena.
French war graves mark each soldier's faith, with a Latin cross, or a stele bearing a Star of David, a crescent, or nothing.
From 1966 to 1968, French military graves from town cemeteries were gathered at Gammarth.
By the French consulate's figures, 1,875 soldiers lie there in individual graves, from both world wars and Indochina.
An ossuary holds 1,220 boxes of remains of unknown soldiers, and the French embassy keeps the site.
Some 25 kilometres from Tunis, near Hammam-Lif, the German war cemetery of Borj Sedria lies on a hillside.
It holds 8,562 German soldiers who died in 1942 and 1943, in battle or as prisoners of war.
After a German and Tunisian agreement in 1966, the cemetery was built from 1973 to 1975.
There are no rows of graves. The remains lie in ossuaries, in six courtyards stepping up the hill.
A stone in Arabic, German and French gives the number, and remembers 104 soldiers never found.
It opened in 1977, and the Folksbund, Germany's war graves commission, keeps it.
The Folksbund itself writes that, given German war crimes, honouring the fallen as heroes was taboo after 1945.
It calls war cemeteries like this one places to learn.
Italy brought its dead home from overseas, Tunisia included, to a memorial in Bari opened in 1967.
So four countries remember with crosses and stars, headstones, crosses and steles, and stone courtyards.
Their figures can't simply be added up. Each body counts in its own way, and some include other wars.
And many people who died in Tunisia have no war cemetery at all.
Tunisians died as soldiers in the French army, and as civilians in their own towns.
Under the German occupation, about 5,000 Jewish men were sent to forced labour, in 32 to about 40 camps.
A US report of June 1943 says their work sites were under nearly constant Allied air attack.
Some were killed, and some Jews of Tunisia were deported to camps in Europe.
The towns were bombed too. Raids on ports, stations and factories left many civilian victims.
By one count, Sousse alone was bombed 39 times in those six months.
The historian Mark Willis writes that most major towns were destroyed or badly damaged, and that this toll is largely forgotten.
No war cemetery gathers these dead. Their memory lives in families, in towns and in archives.
After independence, war memorials came down. In 1957, Tunis removed its monument to the dead of both wars.
Ceremonies go on. In May, Americans gather at Carthage for Memorial Day, and France marks the 8th of May at Gammarth.
In November, France marks the Armistice at Gammarth, and a Remembrance service is held at Medjez-el-Bab.
On Germany's day of mourning, two Sundays before Advent, its ambassador lays a wreath at Borj Sedria.
In 2022, the United States and Tunisia agreed that unknown soldiers buried at Carthage could be exhumed, to try to identify them.
Each of these bodies keeps its records online, so anyone can look up a name.
The persecution of Tunisia's Jews is documented too, some of it written at the time.
Paul Ghez, made to recruit the forced labourers, published his diary in Tunis in 1943.
In Jerusalem, a documentation centre indexes thousands of documents and testimonies.
In Washington, the US Holocaust Memorial Museum records testimonies, Tunisian ones among them.
In Paris, the Shoah Memorial holds a ceremony for the roundup of Tunis, on the 9th of December 1942.
Remembering 1943 in Tunisia means seeing the rows, and the people outside them too.
If you visit a cemetery, check access locally, and go quietly.
Every name in stone, and every name in an archive, belonged to someone.
